questions.stem: A client with a tibial fracture in a circumferential cast reports rapidly worsening pain despite analgesia. Pain increases with passive toe extension, and new paresthesia is present although the distal pulse remains palpable. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings are most consistent with expected post-fracture inflammation because severe pain and paresthesia commonly persist despite analgesia during the first day after casting.","B":"The findings suggest venous thromboembolism because calf pain after immobilization is usually worsened by passive toe movement and commonly produces distal paresthesia.","C":"The findings are concerning for acute compartment syndrome because escalating pain, pain with passive stretch, and sensory change can precede late vascular findings.","D":"The findings suggest isolated superficial nerve compression from the cast because preserved distal pulses make clinically important compartment pressure unlikely."}}
questions.rationale: Acute compartment syndrome can present with escalating pain, pain with passive stretch, and sensory change before late vascular findings appear. A palpable pulse does not exclude the diagnosis because arterial flow may persist until advanced compromise. The pattern requires urgent escalation rather than routine post-fracture observation.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons — 2025 Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Compartment Syndrome
questions.source_detail: Current AAOS guidance emphasizes vigilance for acute compartment syndrome and recognizes that clinical findings alone may be imperfect; worsening pain and sensory change warrant urgent evaluation.
